title: The dog at the threshold
hook: they sleep for years with their dog stretched at the entrance (18:18, 18:25)

segments.voice: Yesterday, fitya, the young men in the cave, and their prayer. Your line was set right our affair. Did you do your one part and let go of the rest? Day four hundred sixty-five.

The young men have prayed, and now they sleep. Inside the cave it's dim. The sun, the surah says, swings past the opening, to the right in the morning and the left in the evening, so it never falls full on them. Someone looking in would swear they were awake. And lying across the entrance, front legs stretched out on the threshold, is a dog. The Qur'an tells you exactly where it lies.

Verse eighteen, in Pickthall's words, ends: "and their dog stretching out his paws on the threshold." Al-wasid, the threshold, the open ground at the mouth of the cave. The dog is lying where a guard would lie. In the same verse, God turns the sleepers over, to the right and to the left, while the dog stays where it is. Then, a few verses on, the story does something unusual. People argue about how many sleepers there were. Some will say three, their dog the fourth. Some say five, their dog the sixth, guessing at the unseen. Some say seven, and their dog the eighth. And the verse ends: say, my Lord knows best their number. Notice: nobody's count leaves out the dog. The men are a number in dispute; the dog is in every version. Verse twenty-five gives a length for the sleep, three hundred years and nine more, and the next verse adds that God knows best how long they stayed. And the animal that followed them in is remembered in a surah recited on Fridays. There's a hadith in Bukhari that fits beside it. A man walking on a hot road found a dog panting and licking the dirt from thirst. He climbed down into a well, filled his leather sock with water, held it in his teeth to climb back up, and gave the dog a drink. God thanked him and forgave him. The companions asked: is there reward for us even with animals? The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said: in every living, breathing creature there is reward. Muslim schools of law differ about dogs, their purity and keeping them in the house. On kindness to them, the hadith is plain.
screen: `AL-WASID: ON THE THRESHOLD.` · `THREE, FIVE OR SEVEN, PLUS THE DOG.` · `THREE HUNDRED YEARS, AND NINE.` · `WATER IN A LEATHER SOCK.` · then, large: `EVEN THE DOG IS REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: The practice is to be kind to a dog, and if there's no dog nearby, to any animal. Sit, and bring to mind an animal you know: a neighbor's dog, a cat on a wall, the pigeons at the bus stop. Picture what it needs: water on a hot day, shade, someone not shooing it. Think of one small, safe kindness you could do for it, or for animals like it, this week. A bowl of water by the door counts. The bell holds the time.
Al-wasid. The threshold where the sleepers' dog stretched its paws, and stayed counted in every version of the story. Today's word.
Your line: even the dog is remembered. Today, do one small kindness for an animal, and notice the creatures you usually walk past. Day four hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims cite the hadith of the man who watered a thirsty dog when teaching kindness to animals; schools of law differ on the ritual purity of dogs and on keeping them indoors.

original.note: Arabic: and their dog stretching out its forelegs at the threshold (18:18).

trapdoor: what you thought: there was a dog in the cave story.
what it means: the dog lies at the threshold through the long sleep, and every count of the sleepers includes it.
what a scholar hears: al-wasid is the threshold or courtyard; 18:22 calls the first two counts 'guessing at the unseen', and some commentators read the third as favored.
recall: to hold back, to hold steady

Editor review (2026-10-01): 18:25's 309 years now paired with 18:26 (God knows best how long they stayed), since Pickthall renders 18:25 '(it is said)'; cut 'every Friday, centuries after' and the 'all schools permit working dogs' claim. Keeper: confirm how to present 18:25.
